readings: The newly inspected Findmypast transcripts establish Thomas Glasgow and Jean Duncan’s Linlithgow banns on 30 March 1701 (groom a servant; witnesses James Craw and William Duncan) and marriage on 4 May 1701. The banns leave both residences as question marks. A third Linlithgow register index names the same couple in 1701 without a day. These are related register entries, not three independent family identifications.

Kirkliston banns dated 22 June 1716 name Thomas Glasgon, resident at Uphall, and Catharine Clerkson, resident at Kirkliston. The named couple, Uphall residence and Margaret’s following 1717 Uphall child entry identify the existing Clarkson household. The FamilySearch-derived duplicate calls this a marriage date; retain the more specific banns label from OPR 667/1, item 5, rather than asserting a ceremony on that day.

Two Findmypast FamilySearch-derived entries name Philip Glasgow, male, baptised 3 June 1711 at Uphall, father Thomas Glasgow and mother Jean Duncan. They corroborate the maintained Scottish child account and do not identify a Mary. The older Mary label is an editorial inconsistency, not a second contemporary child. The separate family citation giving 21 October 1711/Linlithgow remains an unresolved index discrepancy: its underlying page was inaccessible and the present search did not find it. Duplicate transcriptions do not supply independent testimony.

The 15 June 1715 Edinburgh child is already represented by Thomas Glasgow-1243, whose selected father is the Edinburgh baxter Thomas Glasgow-3285. His transcript explicitly calls the father a baxter and indweller. This citation must not be used as another Uphall/Duncan birth or evidence for the proposed Duncan-to-Clarkson succession. The recorded Edinburgh father is retained as a separately identified household; no record establishes its identity with the Uphall father.

father_confidence_changes.basis: Assess John Glasgow-1105 as Thomas Glasgow-1226’s possible father at 30%, previously 22%. The 1701 Thomas/Jean marriage is now anchored in Linlithgow, and the 1716 banns place the Clarkson groom specifically at Uphall before the 1717–1735 child sequence. Together with the Duncan household’s 1704 and 1711 Uphall entries, this makes a local succession more specific than a repeated surname alone. The proposed 1675 Linlithgow child would be about 26 at the 1701 marriage, 41 at the Clarkson banns and 60 at the last 1735 child. This is a coherent, if increasingly late, fatherhood sequence. The modest increase recognises the dated local fit; it does not assert remarriage or a proved identity.
father_confidence_changes.scope: 30% is a subjective assessment of the complete Clarkson-adult → John-1105 proposition. Two identity bridges remain unproved: the 1675 child to the Duncan groom, and the Duncan father to the Clarkson groom. No widowhood, remarital status, age, trade or parent is given in the inspected marriage transcripts. Jean’s death is not established. An unrecorded younger local Thomas remains a serious alternative; Thomas-1311 (1666) and Thomas-3091 (1663) are older compatible rivals. The 1679 Carstairs/Spence groom is not an established identity for this adult. The unverified 1766 memorial contributes no weight. The 1715 Edinburgh citation is excluded from the supporting sequence. Both Thomas accounts remain separate and no biological or profile merge is made.

father_confidence_changes.basis: Assess the existing Thomas Glasgow-1242 → Philip Glasgow-1241 father pair at 72%, previously 52%. The inspected 1711 entries name Philip and the specific Thomas/Jean Duncan couple; the 1701 Linlithgow banns and marriage now independently establish that named adult household. Philip’s maintained 3 June date and Uphall place match exactly. The Mary label that depressed the earlier review is not supported by these entries. Thomas-1242’s retained 1675 Linlithgow child identity gives a plausible age of 26 at the 1701 marriage and 36 at Philip’s baptism, and the same local family route is preferable to an otherwise unidentified Thomas.
father_confidence_changes.scope: 72% is a subjective probable assessment of the complete existing father-profile pair, including the unproved identification of the 1675 child with the 1701 adult. It is not 99% merely because a transcript names a father Thomas. The alternative 21 October/Linlithgow citation remains unresolved. Philip’s Scottish child identity is the basis of this assessment; his later identification with the elder Dublin watchmaker remains uncertain and is not upgraded. No mother, parent selection, birth/death field or live WikiTree value changes. Original parish registers were not inspected.
father_confidence_changes.final_review_reason: Final independent weighting review: the 1701 marriage and exact 1711 child/parental couple identify the Duncan adult well. Correcting the Mary label resolves the child label, not the father’s childhood identity. The connection from that adult to the 1675 Linlithgow child still rests on name, locality and compatible age; neither witnesses nor servant occupation connects him to John/Agnes. Assess the complete father-profile placement at 72%, retaining that identity uncertainty rather than assigning near-certain record-role confidence to the whole chain.

next_test: Inspect the original 1701 and 1716 entries for fuller residence, occupation and marital status; seek Jean Duncan’s burial or a property/probate passage connecting the two households. Reconcile the separate 21 October 1711 citation. An explicit age or family network could distinguish the 1675 child from younger local Thomas namesakes.
